nutshell: Prior animal face identification datasets almost all have fewer than 100 individuals, which makes it impossible to properly evaluate open-set verification of unseen animals. PetFace fixes this by collecting 257,484 unique animal individuals (~1M images) across 13 families and 319 breeds from pet-shop and adoption websites, with fine-grained sex/breed/color annotations, and establishes both closed-set re-identification and open-set (unseen-individual) verification benchmarks.
contributions: PetFace dataset: 257,484 individuals / 1,012,934 images across 13 animal families and 319 breeds - over 110x more individuals than the previous largest animal face dataset (DogFaceNet, 1,393 dogs) - built via labor-efficient internet sourcing (pet-shop and adoption websites) rather than manual photography, with a two-stage automated+manual filtering pipeline (~100 human-hours of manual review).

Fine-grained annotations: sex for 94% of individuals, breed labels for 8 families, and manually-verified color/pattern labels for 11 families, enabling a same-breed ('fine-grained') verification benchmark in addition to standard cross-breed verification.

Two benchmark protocols with careful data splitting: closed-set re-identification (classification over seen identities) and open-set verification (pairwise same/different-identity prediction on identities never seen in training, with train/val/test separated by image source to prevent background/environment leakage).

Demonstrates that models trained on PetFace generalize better than models trained on narrower prior datasets in direct cross-dataset comparisons (e.g. beats CTai/CZoo on chimp, beats DogFaceNet/Flickr-dog on dog, including beating those datasets' own in-dataset numbers), and beats general-purpose models (ImageNet, CLIP) and the prior best animal-identification foundation model (MegaDescriptor) on verification, fine-grained breed-level verification, and generalization to three animal families never seen in training (Parrot, Lacertilia, Squirrel).
deficiencies: Joint training across all 13 families (their proposed 'integrated' model) has mixed effects the paper doesn't investigate further: several families improve substantially (Cat Top-1 54.29%->70.30%) while others get meaningfully worse (Chimp 43.27%->34.30%, Parakeet 62.19%->44.78%) - the paper notes 'room to improve' but offers no analysis of why certain families degrade or any mitigation for the apparent class/family imbalance.

Center loss fails dramatically in the main re-identification comparison (Table 2: 9.81% average Top-1, literally 0% on both Cat and Dog) and is included with only a brief note that it 'does not learn sufficient discriminative features,' with no deeper diagnosis of this near-total failure mode on a headline benchmark table.

Sex and breed labels come directly from pet-shop/adoption-site metadata rather than independent verification - the paper explicitly states only color/pattern labels were manually checked/annotated 'because images alone do not allow us to accurately determine an animal's sex or breed' - so an unknown amount of label noise from self-reported source metadata may exist in two of the three annotation types.

All images come from pet-shop and adoption websites (posed, largely front-facing, single-animal photos), a narrower and more curated distribution than the in-the-wild or camera-trap conditions relevant to some of the paper's own motivating use cases (habitat surveys, wildlife monitoring) - robustness to that domain gap is untested; only cross-dataset and cross-family generalization within similarly curated photo distributions is measured.
notable: The similarity-distribution diagnostic (Fig. 5, plotting positive vs. negative cosine-similarity histograms for CLIP vs. MegaDescriptor vs. their own model on the same cat test set) makes separation quality visually obvious in a way a single AUC number doesn't - a simple, reusable verification-model diagnostic. Also notable: ResNet-50 beats both ViT-B/32 and Swin-B under an identical training recipe on this dataset (Table 5), a mild counter-point to the 'transformers beat CNNs' pattern common in the human-ReID literature elsewhere in this batch - plausibly because animal-face datasets are smaller and lack the huge unlabeled pretraining corpora (e.g. LUPerson) that make transformers competitive for human ReID.
